name: Commercial Modernism
summary: Modernism in the service of selling, as in the posters of Cassandre, Kauffer, Bernhard, Matter and Beall. One product or symbol as the hero, shown big and from a bold viewpoint; strong diagonals and a low horizon; smooth airbrushed modelling between the colours of one Wada combination; geometric lettering built into the image; a short slogan and the brand name set large.

principles.title: The product is the hero
principles.rule: One object fills the poster: 40-65% of the canvas height, or a crop that runs off one edge. Remove everything else, as Bernhard reduced the Priester poster to two matches and a name.

principles.title: One bold viewpoint
principles.rule: Show the object from where it looks most powerful: a low horizon (lower 20-35% of the canvas) so it looms, a one-point perspective that drives the eye to a vanishing point, or a frontal monument. One viewpoint per piece.
principles.source: Cassandre, Étoile du Nord and Normandie (research.md 2.2)

principles.title: Diagonals carry energy
principles.rule: At least one dominant diagonal or converging line set, at 15-40 degrees from the horizontal or vertical. Static pieces still imply movement: speed lines, rails, beams, wings.
principles.source: Implied motion (research.md 3); Kauffer, Soaring to Success (research.md 2.2)

principles.title: Airbrush, within one combination
principles.rule: Volume comes from smooth two-stop gradients between colours of the piece's Wada combination (plus Black and White), inside hard stencil edges. Never a gradient to a colour outside the combination, never on lettering, never a drop shadow.

principles.title: Lettering is part of the picture
principles.rule: The brand name and slogan sit in planned zones (a band at the top or bottom, or along a perspective line) and are as large as the image allows. Geometric sans or deco display; the brand word may be set in capitals.

principles.title: Few words, said once
principles.rule: A slogan of 2-7 words and the brand name. Body copy only in print ads and pages, never on the poster image itself.
principles.source: Pieters & Wedel (2004) on text and brand elements (research.md 3)

principles.title: Machine-age polish, not nostalgia
principles.rule: Clean edges and precise curves, like a well-made product. No fake wear, paper stains, faded inks or period costume: the piece should feel new, built with the 1930s method (MAYA).

layers.do: One Wada combination per piece, chosen from art.json recommendedCombinations. Ground from the combination's bg; the hero object in its dark colour or Black; the accent on one object. Two-stop airbrush gradients only between colours of that combination, Black and White.
layers.dont: Mix combinations, use gradients with colours outside the combination, multi-stop rainbows, glows, drop shadows, metallic or chrome effects.

layers.do: Geometric sans or deco display faces (typography.json newPairings, then schibsted). Brand word in capitals with wide tracking; slogan in sentence case. Three sizes per piece.
layers.dont: Calligraphic or soft rounded faces, handwriting, distressed 'vintage' fonts, more than two families.

layers.do: One object at 40-65% of canvas height; a low horizon or a clear vanishing point; lettering in one or two bands (top 10-18% and/or bottom 18-28% of the canvas); 5-7% margins.
layers.dont: Several products in one poster, centred-everything symmetry without a viewpoint, text floating over busy areas, boxes and borders.

layers.do: Hard-edged stencil shapes, no outlines; volume by airbrush gradient and by a light side and a shade side; streamline curves (teardrops, long tapering forms) against straight diagonals.
layers.dont: Ink outlines, hand-wobble, texture overlays, detailed scenes, people as faceless bendy figures, heroic muscular figures.

layers.do: Smooth, elegant cubic eases; slow push-ins (scale 1 to 1.06 over 4-6 s); objects gliding in along their diagonal; speed lines sweeping; lettering wiping on (motion.json).
layers.dont: Bouncy springs, wobble, shaking, more than one moving object, spinning, parallax beyond 4% of the canvas.

layers.do: Photomontage in the manner of Herbert Matter: one large cut-out photo (a face, a hand, the product) against a small scene or a flat ground, a scale jump of at least 4:1; duotone or posterized in the combination's colours.
layers.dont: Full-bleed unedited stock, soft-focus lifestyle photos, many small photos.

layers.do: A short, confident slogan to one person, with a specific fact (a time, a route, a place). The brand name set large beside it. A direct call to action where the format needs one.
layers.dont: Exclamation marks, period pastiche ('Ye olde', 'Swell!'), superlatives without proof, long paragraphs on the image.

notes.curves: Mixed on purpose: streamline curves and teardrops sit against sharp diagonals, bows and wedges, which carry speed but lose some liking (curvature).
notes.simplicity: The Sachplakat rule is one object and a name; low complexity is the method, not a by-product (simplicity).
notes.maya: A poster that looks like a poster, a recognisable product, one surprising viewpoint; MAYA is named after Raymond Loewy, a streamline designer of this period (maya).
notes.nature: Machine-age forms and smooth airbrush have none of the mid-range fractal roughness people like in nature (fractals).
notes.handmade: The originals were painted by hand, but the look aims at machine polish; it gives up the handmade-warmth effect (handmade).
notes.colour: Wada combinations with deep blues and clear reds suit it; the period's ochres and browns need care on large fields (colour-valence).
notes.glance: Built to be read from moving vehicles: one silhouette, high figure-ground contrast, a big name (first-impression).

beyondPreference.wins: Attention to the picture, the words and the brand
beyondPreference.why: In eye-tracking of 1,363 print ads, each of brand, picture and text had its own effect on attention; the picture captured attention independent of its size, while enlarging the picture did not raise total attention and a larger text area and headline did. One strong product image plus large lettering uses both.

beyondPreference.wins: Stopping power through design, not clutter
beyondPreference.why: Design complexity (an elaborate, creative layout) increased attention and liking, while feature complexity (dense detail, many edges and colours) hurt brand attention. Bold perspective is design complexity with few features.
beyondPreference.source: Pieters, Wedel & Batra (2010), Journal of Marketing 74(5)

beyondPreference.wins: A sense of movement in a still image
beyondPreference.why: Still images that imply motion activated the brain's motion areas (MT/MST) more than images at rest; later work suggests low-level features such as oriented lines contribute. Diagonals and speed lines use this.
beyondPreference.source: Kourtzi & Kanwisher (2000), Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience 12(1); Lorteije et al. (2011)

beyondPreference.wins: Cultural meaning: modern, efficient, going places
beyondPreference.why: Streamlining was styling as much as engineering: products were shaped to look fast and modern. The style borrows that association for travel, transport, energy and premium everyday goods.

line.edge: Hard and clean: every shape has a crisp edge, as if cut from a stencil. Softness happens inside a shape (airbrush), never at its edge.

speedLines.taper: Each line in a set is thinner and shorter than the last (about 10-15% per step), or the set tapers toward the vanishing point.
speedLines.spacing: Equal spacing within a set, 2-4 x the line width.
speedLines.ends: Round or cut square; never arrowheads.
speedLines.direction: Parallel to the object's direction of travel, or converging on the vanishing point.

thinRules.use: A single thin rule to separate the lettering band, or a short accent bar beside the brand name.

rules: No outlines around objects or letters.
No wobble, no brush texture, no dashed lines.
Speed lines never cross the hero object; they run behind it or beside it.

families.streamline: Teardrops, long tapering curves, ellipses in perspective, quarter-circle ends (locomotive noses, hulls, wings, bottles). Curves are smooth arcs or quadratic curves, never irregular blobs.
families.diagonal: Wedges, bows, rays, rails and beams: straight edges meeting at sharp angles, set on the diagonals of the composition.

shape.ratio: Roughly two-thirds of the hero object's outline is streamline curve and one-third straight diagonal; the background carries the straight lines (rails, rays, horizon).
shape.silhouette: The hero object must read as itself in solid black at 5% of its size (the 50 ms test).

detailCount.note: Small details (portholes, windows, rivets) count as one each; a repeated row counts as one.

rules: No organic blobs or hand-cut edges: precision is the point.
Perspective is consistent: all receding edges of one object meet at one vanishing point (two at most).
One accent-coloured object per piece.

use.image: none; or a circle / porthole mask for one featured image
use.band: none: lettering bands run edge to edge

corners.print: Poster bands and image boxes are square-cut.

low.use: The object looms over the viewer (Normandie). Default for products, vehicles, buildings.

high.use: Looking down on a route, a map or a table of products.

eye.use: Only for a one-point tunnel view (Étoile du Nord): rails or a road meeting at the centre.

vanishingPoints.onePoint: Vanishing point on the horizon, within the middle third horizontally, or exactly on the brand name or the accent.
vanishingPoints.twoPoint: At least one vanishing point off-canvas, so angles stay dramatic but not distorted (receding edges 15-40 degrees from horizontal).
vanishingPoints.rule: The vanishing point is a focal point: put the accent, a star, a sun or the brand there.

diagonal.direction: Rising left to right for progress and departure (a rule of thumb, not a finding); falling right to left for arrival.

perspective.scaleJump: Montage pieces: the near object is at least 4 x the size of the far scene behind it (Matter).

airbrush.colours: Both stops are colours of the piece's Wada combination, or Wada Black / Wada White. Never a colour from another combination, never a tint made by opacity over another colour.

lengthPct.note: A gradient runs across at least 25% of the shape's width or height, so it reads as light, not as an edge glow.

airbrush.maxObjectsNote: At most 4 objects carry gradients (the faces of one object count as one), plus one sky or ground gradient and one sea or floor gradient.
airbrush.maxAreaNote: Share of the canvas covered by modelled objects. A sky or floor gradient is not counted, but it must be gentle: its two stops are neighbouring light colours of the combination, or a dark colour and Black.
airbrush.lightSide: One light direction per piece (usually upper left). Lit faces run from the lighter colour; shade faces from the darker. A hard split between a lit face and a shade face along a ridge (bow, nose, bottle shoulder) is the signature move.
airbrush.sky: A sky or ground gradient may run from the combination's lightest colour at the horizon to its bg (or a neighbouring light colour) at the top.
never: Glows and halos outside a shape
airbrush.svg: linearGradient or radialGradient with exactly two stop elements; stop-color values from the palette only.

bottomBand.use: Default: a solid band (ink or the combination's dark colour) with brand, slogan and details. Normandie, Étoile du Nord.

topBand.use: Brand name across the top when the object sits low.

onPerspective.use: Words set along a perspective line or framing the image (the Étoile du Nord border). Use for one short word only.

serial.use: A word that builds across a series (Dubo, Dubon, Dubonnet). Use for campaigns of 3 pieces.

brandWord.note: The brand name is large enough to read at the poster's viewing distance on its own.

rules: Lettering never sits over an airbrush gradient or a busy area; it sits on a flat band or flat ground.
Words and image share one edge or one axis: a band edge, the horizon, or a perspective line.

composition.grid: Thirds: horizon on a third (or lower), hero object on the centre axis or a vertical third, lettering in a band.
composition.motifMeasure: Height of the hero object as a share of canvas height; a crop may run off one edge.

placements.use: Low horizon, object frontal and looming, centred; lettering band below (Normandie).
One-point perspective, rails or road converging on the accent at the vanishing point (Étoile du Nord).
Sachplakat: the product alone on a flat ground, large, with the brand name above or below. No perspective needed.
A large cut-out photo or shape close up, with a small scene far behind (Matter); scale jump at least 4:1.
The object or a flock of repeated shapes rising along one diagonal (Kauffer, Soaring to Success).

composition.pairing: Slogan and image are a pair: the image shows the product at its best; the slogan adds the fact or the promise the image cannot show.
rules: One hero object; a second object only as setting (sea, rails, sun).
Lettering bands run edge to edge.
The accent sits on the focal point or the vanishing point.

ground.from: combination bg (may airbrush toward the combination's lightest colour)

object.from: combination ink/dark colour or Wada Black, airbrushed between them

band.from: Wada Black or the combination's dark colour

paper.use: Highlights, lettering on the band, speed lines, wake.

accent.limit: One object (or one group, such as a ship's funnels).

method: Start from what the product is made of or where it goes: sea and sky (blues), sun and brass (yellows, ochres), signals and enamel (reds).
Pick a combination of 3-4 colours from recommendedCombinations whose light-mode inkUse is 'body', so the dark colour can carry the object and the band text.
Assign: lightest colour to the ground or sky, darkest to the object and band, the strongest hue to the accent.
Check that the object's darkest face against the ground is at least 3:1 and band text at least 4.5:1.

recommendedCombinations.why: Cream ground, brass accent and a deep travel blue: the classic railway and liner scheme.
Pale morning sky over a dark sea blue, with an orange signal accent; very high contrast (7.5:1).
Near-primary red, yellow and blue: the Sachplakat palette for a single product on a bright ground.
Red, black and cream, the most common object-poster scheme; 12.8:1 ink contrast.
Navy and red on a warm ground, close to the ocean-liner posters.
Sunlit golden ground for departures and energy; check text contrast (4.7:1).
Yellow ground with black and one red: maximum glance clarity for packaged goods.
Warm buff with black and deep blue: corporate and editorial, Fortune-cover warmth.
Grey, black and red: the restrained industrial scheme of Beall's and Kauffer's posters.
Alpine sky and lake blues on bright yellow: suits Matter-style tourism montage.
Earthy and corporate for industry, materials and engineering.
Black object on lemon with a peach-red accent: loud, simple retail posters.

rules: One combination per piece.
Gradients only between colours of that combination, plus Black and White (airbrush).
Text on the band uses Wada White or the combination's lightest colour; text on the ground uses the combination's text role (AA contrast).

texture.airbrush: Smooth two-stop gradients are the only tonal device (see airbrush).

halftone.use: Only inside photomontage (duotone photos). Never as illustration shading.

texture.grain: None. No paper texture, stains, fold lines or faded ink: they turn the style into pastiche.

avoid.why: The visual language of 1930s totalitarian propaganda, including Hohlwein's Nazi-era posters (research.md 5).
Common in period advertising and harmful; depict real places and people with dignity or use objects instead.
Women as ornament was a period cliché; show the product or the experience.
Pastiche; a sun or beam must mean something in the piece.
Worn out and cold; show the actual machine or product.

recipe: Write the one message in a sentence (W1).
List everything you could show. Cross out all but the product (or the one object that stands for the service).
Choose the viewpoint that makes that object most powerful: monument (low horizon), tunnel (vanishing point), object (flat), montage (scale jump) or diagonal (art.json composition.placements).
Pick one light direction and model the object with two-stop airbrush gradients: a lit face and a shade face.
Put the accent on the focal point (vanishing point, funnel, cap, label).
Add the brand name in a band, as large as the band allows, then the slogan.
Test: shrink to 5% and blur. Do the object and the brand name still read? (glance)

checklist: One hero object at 40-65% of canvas height (or cropped by one edge).
One viewpoint: horizon placed deliberately; receding lines meet at 1-2 vanishing points.
At least one dominant diagonal (15-40 degrees) or converging line set.
Airbrush gradients: two stops, colours of one combination only, at most 4 modelled objects plus sky and floor, none on lettering.
Lettering in a planned zone; brand name large; slogan 2-7 words.
Accent on one object, at the focal point.

motion.character: Streamlined and assured: objects glide along their diagonals on long, smooth eases, the camera pushes in slowly, speed lines sweep past, lettering wipes on like a sign being revealed. Nothing bounces, wobbles or overshoots.

glide.use: Default arrival for the hero object along its diagonal. Damping ratio 1.0: settles without overshoot.

precise.use: UI feedback: buttons, toggles, cards. Damping ratio about 1.01.

heavy.use: Large objects (a ship, a locomotive) arriving slowly, with weight. Damping ratio about 1.03.

streamline.use: Arrivals: fast start, long elegant settle (ease-out quint). Default.

cruise.use: Moves that start and stop on screen: push-ins, pans, wipes.

sweep.use: Looping sine-like moves: beams sweeping, a sun rising and settling.

depart.use: Things leaving: accelerate away along the diagonal, toward the vanishing point.

glide.use: The hero object enters along its own diagonal or toward the viewer from the vanishing point.

pushIn.use: Slow camera push toward the object or the vanishing point. One per piece.

speedLines.use: Speed lines draw on from the object outward (scaleX 0 to 1 from their inner end), shortest last.

wipe.use: Brand name and slogan revealed by a hard-edged mask moving left to right, like a sign. No fade.

bandSlide.use: The lettering band slides in from its edge before the words wipe on.

sweep.use: A searchlight or sun ray sweeping back and forth (loop).

serial.use: Dubonnet-style sequence: 3 frames build one idea (a word completes, a glass fills, an object gains colour); hold the last.

depart.use: Exit toward the vanishing point, scaling down to 60-80%.

durations.formula: duration = 350 ms + 0.5 ms per pixel travelled (capped at 1200 ms); push-ins and loops are exempt

order: accent (no move; it is already in place)
choreography.settleBeforeText: Lettering starts when the object is about 80% settled, so the image lands first and the name follows.

loop.endsOn: The full poster as a still frame: object settled, all lettering visible.

rules: No overshoot, bounce or wobble: every spring is critically damped or heavier.
Objects move along the composition's diagonals or toward/away from the vanishing point, never sideways at random.
Lettering wipes on with a hard edge; it never fades, bounces or scales.
One thing moves at a time; push-ins may run under one other move.
Loops end on a still frame that works as the poster.
With reduced motion: show the final frame; push-ins, sweeps and loops stop.

typography.character: Geometric and confident: letters built from circles, squares and straight strokes (the Futura and Kabel generation of 1927), or high-contrast Art Deco display letters. The brand name is set big, in capitals, with wide tracking, as part of the picture; the slogan is short and bold; everything else is small.

construction.want: Geometric: round O, near-circular bowls, straight stems
construction.why: Matches the streamline curves and straight diagonals of the art; this is the letterform of the period (Futura 1927, Kabel 1927).

strokes.want: Monoline for text; very high contrast for one display word
strokes.why: Monoline reads at a distance; deco contrast (Limelight, Bodoni) gives the brand name glamour.

terminals.why: Echo the stencil edges; rounded terminals read as soft and friendly.

proportions.want: Contrasting widths: wide round letters, narrow E, F, S
proportions.why: Classical geometric proportions give capitals their stately rhythm when tracked out.

xHeight.want: Low to moderate for display, moderate for text
xHeight.why: Period geometric faces have low x-heights; keep body text sizes generous to compensate.

capitals.want: Well-drawn capitals that track well at 0.08-0.2 em
capitals.why: The brand word is set in capitals.

avoid: Novelty Art Deco faces with stripes or inlines for anything but one word

jost.why: New pairing. A Futura-like geometric family with weights 100-900: the period letterform for slogan, brand and text.

limelight-jost.why: New pairing. High-contrast Art Deco display for the brand word over Jost: travel, hospitality, theatre.

bodoni-jost.why: New pairing. Bodoni display over geometric sans, after Brodovitch's Harper's Bazaar: fashion, editorial, premium.

schibsted.why: Of the existing pairings, the sturdiest grotesque: heavy weights carry a Bernhard-style brand name.

bricolage-figtree.why: Bold grotesque display with a geometric-humanist body; its ink traps are more contemporary than period, which keeps it fresh.

instrument.why: The condensed high-contrast serif works for editorial and fashion pieces in the Brodovitch manner.

plex.why: Engineered and industrial; for B2B and technical products where the modernism is corporate (CCA).

fraunces-commissioner.why: Heavy soft serif recalls 1920s display faces such as Cooper Black; for food and drink only, one weight.

source.why: Humanist and bookish; it has none of the geometric construction the style depends on.

young-onest.why: Soft old-style serif: warm and friendly, opposite to the machine-age polish.

nunito.why: Rounded terminals read as soft and casual; the style needs crisp edges.

alegreya.why: Calligraphic letterforms from the pen; the style's letters are constructed, not written.

newPairings.name: Geometric Poster
newPairings.mood: The 1927 geometric sans, revived: confident, clean and modern-classic. One family in many weights; hierarchy from size, weight and tracked capitals.
newPairings.bestFor: Commercial Modernism posters, transport, energy, products, corporate campaigns.

display.case: Sentence case for slogans; capitals with 0.1-0.2 em tracking for the brand word
display.notes: Inspired by the German geometric sans faces of the 1920s, Futura in particular; not a digitisation of Futura. Variable version made with Mirko Velimirovic (2020).

body.notes: Low x-height: set body text one step larger than usual.

newPairings.name: Deco Marquee
newPairings.mood: A high-contrast Art Deco display face for the brand word, with a geometric sans for everything else. Glamour kept to one word.
newPairings.bestFor: Travel, hotels, theatre and cinema, drinks, events.

display.case: Capitals or title for the brand word only (1-3 words); never for sentences
display.notes: Single weight (400). Extreme contrast: use at 24 px / 18 pt and above.

body.notes: Jost 700 sets the slogan; Limelight sets only the brand word.

newPairings.name: Bazaar Editorial
newPairings.mood: Didone display over geometric sans: the 1930s fashion-magazine pairing. Elegant, high contrast, lots of white space.
newPairings.bestFor: Fashion, beauty, editorial, galleries, premium goods.

display.case: Sentence case; italic for one emphasised word
display.notes: Use the large optical size for headlines; hairlines break up below about 18 px at small opsz settings.

handwritten.why: Streamlined, engineered lettering is the point of the style; handwriting reads as a different era and a different promise.

typeWithArt.zones: Type lives in the lettering zones in art.json (bands, perspective lines); it never sits over an airbrush gradient.
typeWithArt.brandScale: The brand word spans 45-90% of the canvas width, or its cap height is at least 1/6 of the hero object's height.
typeWithArt.alignment: Align to one band edge or to the horizon. Centred is allowed for a single brand word on a symmetrical monument composition; slogans and details stay left-aligned.
typeWithArt.perspective: One word may follow a perspective line or frame the image (Étoile du Nord); set it in capitals and skew it with the grid, never distort it freely.
typeWithArt.colour: White or the combination's lightest colour on the dark band; Black or the combination's dark colour on light ground. Never gradient-filled letters.

sizes.viewingDistance: Sign-industry rule of thumb: about 1 inch (25 mm) of letter height for every 10 feet (3 m) of viewing distance for basic legibility; double it for comfortable reading. Period posters for roadside viewing (Dubonnet) were sized for passing traffic.

measure.source: Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style (45-75); shorter here because geometric faces with low x-heights tire the eye sooner (rule of thumb)

setting.case: Slogans and text in sentence case. Capitals for the brand word and labels of one to three words, always tracked out.
setting.rag: Ragged right; balanced two-line slogans (text-wrap: balance); no single-word last lines.
setting.numbers: Times, dates and routes in the body face's tabular figures or the mono.

rules: Geometric letterforms, set big and with confidence.
Brand word in tracked capitals; slogan in sentence case.
Three sizes and two weights per piece (a deco display face counts as one weight).
Type sits in planned zones, never over gradients.
No handwriting, rounded or distressed fonts.
